summary: Concurrent refresh race: ValidToken/playerCommand/Search all call c.refresh() with the lock released, so simultaneous callers fire duplicate refresh_token grants; if Spotify rotates the refresh token the loser persists a now-invalid one.
scenario: The Stage's getOAuthToken callback (GET /api/spotify/token) fires at the same moment a player command hits a 401 during a multi-hour game. Both goroutines see an expired token and each POST grant_type=refresh_token concurrently. Spotify may rotate the refresh token; goroutine A stores the new refresh token, goroutine B (using the old rt) either fails or overwrites c.refreshToken with a value Spotify has already invalidated -> next refresh returns invalid_grant -> forced full re-OAuth mid-event.
suggested_fix: Serialize refresh with a singleflight/refresh-in-progress guard (e.g. golang.org/x/sync/singleflight keyed constant, or a dedicated refreshMu held across the whole refresh) so only one refresh runs and late callers reuse its result.

summary: ValidToken silently returns an expired access token when there is no refresh token, instead of erroring.
scenario: After a boot with only an access token pushed (no refresh token, e.g. an implicit-style seed) and >1h elapsed, the Stage fetches /api/spotify/token and receives a dead token with HTTP 200. The Web Playback SDK then fails opaquely (401 on the SDK side) rather than the endpoint returning a clear 409 telling the operator to re-auth.
suggested_fix: When !hasRefresh and the token is past expiry (c.clock().After(exp)), return an error like the not-authenticated case rather than returning the stale token.

summary: playlistID is concatenated directly into the API URL path without url.PathEscape; safe today only because the sole caller (admin.extractPlaylistID) validates it against ^[a-zA-Z0-9]+$. No defense at the point of use.
scenario: GetPlaylistTracks is an exported method on *spotify.Client. If any future caller passes a playlistID containing '/', '?', or '..' without the admin-layer regex, the attacker controls the request path against api.spotify.com (path traversal into other Spotify endpoints, or query-string injection). Currently non-exploitable via the HTTP surface because importPlaylist gates on the regex, but the invariant lives in a different package.
suggested_fix: Escape at the point of use: endpoint := c.apiBase + "/playlists/" + url.PathEscape(playlistID) + "/items?" + q.Encode(), and/or validate the ID inside the spotify package.

summary: OAuth state cookie is set without the Secure attribute; at a hacker-conference LAN with the plaintext HTTP redirect URI (default http://127.0.0.1:8777), a network attacker can read the state cookie and the callback 'code' in transit. (Note: the CSRF state/cookie logic itself is correct — cookie Path=/auth/spotify DOES match the /auth/spotify/callback request per RFC 6265, missing-cookie short-circuits before want.Value deref, empty-state is rejected.)
scenario: OAuth flow runs over plaintext HTTP (the shipped SPOTIFY_REDIRECT_URI is http://). A passive attacker on the conference LAN sniffs the yfi_spotify_state cookie and the authorization code from the callback URL, defeating the state binding and potentially replaying the code before the legit callback consumes it.
suggested_fix: Serve the OAuth endpoints over TLS and set Secure: true on the state cookie (Secure works on localhost in modern browsers). Document that the redirect URI must be https in any non-loopback deployment.
